newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission set to propose new anti-smoking measures.
newsitem.headline: Commission set to propose new anti-smoking measures.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to propose within the next few weeks new measures to discourage smoking in the European Union.
The proposal has not yet been finalised, but the Commission is looking closely at a recent series of recommendations made by an EU group of cancer experts, Commission spokeswoman Barbara Nolan said.
That group, set up under the EU's "Europe Against Cancer" programme, called for new limits on nicotine content, controls on additives and stronger health warnings on tobacco labels.
"Anything that can contribute to reducing tobacco consumption will be considered," Nolan told Reuters.
The initiative has been launched by EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn, who has waged a long-running battle campaign to cut down on tobacco-related deaths.

He has pushed, so far unsuccessfully, to extend the EU's ban on television advertising of tobacco products to cover all advertising, draft directive COM(92)196. He has also sharply criticised several advertising campaigns of U.S. tobacco giant Philip Morris.
Flynn recently called U.S. President Bill Clinton "courageous" for his plan to impose new controls on tobacco sales and advertising.

Nolan said the full Commission was tentatively set to have a first debate on Flynn's proposals on October 30. The Commission will discuss at the same time proposals by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler on reforms to the EU's tobacco farm subsidy programme.

Flynn is not convinced ending tobacco subsidies would cut down on smoking since buyers would simply rely on imports, Nolan said. However, he would like to ensure that low-grade products are not "dumped" on third markets and to promote programmes that help tobacco farmers turn to other crops, she said.

The group of cancer experts recommended that the nicotine content of cigarettes be limited to a maximum of one milligram from December 31, 1997, and then reduced by 10 percent per year until the level is brought down to 0.5 mg.

They said additives other than tobacco should be banned unless they are proven to be nontoxic and that health warnings on tobacco products should be strengthened and include a toll-free number for obtaining information on smoking and its health consequences.
Generic packaging of tobacco products should be introduced by the end of the year 2000 and exports of unlabelled products or those with high tar and nicotine content should be stopped, they added.
They said the proposed ban on tobacco advertising should be adopted without delay and self-service displays and vending machines should be barred to reduce consumption by young people.
